items.label: Minimum safe internal temperature for all poultry, whole or ground, and for reheated leftovers (74°C).
Safe internal temperature for ground beef, pork, veal, and lamb (71°C). Ground poultry needs 165°F.
Safe internal temperature for steaks, roasts, and chops of beef, pork, veal, and lamb, followed by a 3 minute rest (63°C).
The highest safe refrigerator temperature (4°C). Aim for 34 to 38°F.
Freezer temperature. Frozen food should arrive and stay frozen solid at this temperature or below (-18°C).
Maximum time perishable food should sit at room temperature. Only 1 hour when it is above 90°F.
How long leftovers keep in the refrigerator.
Refrigerator thawing time for every 4 to 5 pounds of turkey. A 15 pound bird needs about 3 days.
Standard temperature for roasting meats, poultry, and vegetables.
The most common baking temperature for cakes, cookies, and quick breads.
Common temperature for pies, tarts, and fritters.
Typical temperature for pizza and other high heat baking.
Very high heat for crisp pizza crusts and crusty breads.
Smoke point of extra virgin olive oil. Refined or light olive oil handles higher heat, around 465°F.
Freezing point of water (0°C).
Boiling point of water at sea level (100°C). Water boils about 1°F lower for every 500 feet of elevation.
Thread stage. Syrup forms thin threads, used for syrups and glazes.
Soft ball stage, used for fudge and pralines.
Sugar begins to caramelize and turn amber.
Useful for measuring small volumes.
Common conversion for spices and small amounts.
Standard metric cup used on nutrition labels.
A common unit of liquid measurement in the United States.
Weight of one pound in grams.
Approximate number of drops in a teaspoon. It depends on the dropper and the liquid.
Water to rice for long grain white rice (2 parts water to 1 part rice).
Typical amount of salt per 1 cup of all-purpose flour in baking.
Common fat percentage in ground beef for burgers (80/20).
Resting time for steaks after cooking. Large roasts need 15 to 20 minutes.
The golden ratio. Interesting to experiment with in the kitchen, though not a proven cooking rule.
